question: What is the most important reason for doing a vehicle inspection?
choice_b: Safety, for yourself and for other road users
choice_c: To keep the paint clean
choice_d: To satisfy the dispatcher
explanation: The manual states safety is the most important reason you inspect your vehicle, safety for yourself and for other road users.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.1 Why Inspect

question: If federal or state inspectors judge a vehicle to be unsafe, what will they do?
choice_a: Require the driver to attend a class
choice_b: Issue only a verbal warning
choice_c: Impound the cargo only
choice_d: Put it "out of service" until it is fixed
explanation: The manual states that if inspectors judge a vehicle unsafe, they will put it out of service until it is fixed.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.1 Why Inspect

question: Which of these should you check during a trip when you stop, according to the manual's list of critical items?
choice_b: Only the engine oil level
choice_c: Only the windshield wipers
choice_d: Tires, wheels/rims, brakes, and lights and reflectors
explanation: The manual lists tires/wheels/rims, brakes, lights/reflectors, brake and electrical connections to the trailer, coupling devices, and cargo securement devices as critical items to check when stopped during a trip.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.2 Types of Vehicle Inspection

question: Why should you keep a copy of your after-trip vehicle inspection report in the vehicle for one day?
choice_a: It is required only for insurance purposes
choice_b: So it can be mailed to the DMV
choice_c: So the next driver can learn about any problems you found
choice_d: It has no real purpose beyond record-keeping
explanation: The manual states keeping a copy of the report in the vehicle for one day lets the next driver learn about any problems found.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.7 After-trip Inspection and Report

question: What is the minimum tread depth required in every major groove on front tires?
choice_b: 2/32 inch
choice_c: 4/32 inch
choice_d: 6/32 inch
explanation: The manual states you need at least 4/32-inch tread depth in every major groove on front tires.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Tire Problems

question: What is the minimum tread depth required on tires other than the front tires?
choice_b: 1/32 inch
choice_c: 6/32 inch
choice_d: 4/32 inch
explanation: The manual states you need 2/32-inch tread depth on other (non-front) tires.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Tire Problems

question: What does the manual say about re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires on a bus?
choice_a: They are only allowed on the rear wheels of a car
choice_b: There is no restriction for buses
choice_c: They are prohibited on the front wheels of a bus
choice_d: They are required on the front wheels of a bus
explanation: The manual states re-grooved, recapped, or retreaded tires on the front wheels of a bus are prohibited.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Tire Problems

question: Which tire combination is listed as a defect to watch for?
choice_b: Radial and bias-ply tires used together
choice_c: Matching tire brands on the same axle
choice_d: Two new radial tires on the steer axle
explanation: The manual lists radial and bias-ply tires used together as a tire problem to check for.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Tire Problems

question: Rust around wheel nuts may indicate what problem?
choice_b: The tire is overinflated
choice_c: Nothing of concern
choice_d: The wheel is brand new
explanation: The manual notes rust around wheel nuts may mean the nuts are loose and tightness should be checked.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Wheel and Rim Problems

question: After a tire has been changed, what should you do a short while later?
choice_b: Replace the tire again
choice_c: Drive an additional 500 miles before checking anything
choice_d: Stop and re-check tightness of the nuts
explanation: The manual instructs that after a tire has been changed, you should stop a short while later and re-check the tightness of the nuts.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Wheel and Rim Problems

question: If one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring, what happens?
choice_a: Only a written warning is issued
choice_b: Nothing; it is considered a minor cosmetic issue
choice_c: It will put the vehicle "out of service"
choice_d: The spring must simply be repainted
explanation: The manual states that if one-fourth or more of the leaves are missing from a leaf spring, it will put the vehicle out of service.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Suspension System Defects

question: Which of the following is described as a suspension system defect to look for?
choice_b: Properly inflated tires
choice_c: A clean windshield
choice_d: Spring hangers that allow movement of the axle from its proper position
explanation: The manual lists spring hangers that allow movement of the axle from proper position as a suspension defect.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Suspension System Defects

question: How much steering wheel play can make a vehicle hard to steer, according to the manual?
choice_b: Any amount of play at all
choice_c: More than 10 degrees (about 2 inches of movement at the rim of a 20-inch wheel)
choice_d: More than 45 degrees
explanation: The manual states steering wheel play of more than 10 degrees, approximately 2 inches movement at the rim of a 20-inch steering wheel, can make it hard to steer.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Steering System Defects

question: Why is a broken exhaust system especially dangerous?
choice_b: It can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth
choice_c: It causes a flat tire
choice_d: It overheats the brakes
explanation: The manual warns a broken exhaust system can let poison fumes into the cab or sleeper berth.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Exhaust System Defects

question: What warning devices for parked vehicles must be carried as emergency equipment?
choice_a: Three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses or 3 liquid burning flares
choice_b: A red flag only
choice_c: A flashlight only
choice_d: A first-aid kit only
explanation: The manual lists warning devices for parked vehicles as three reflective triangles, or at least 6 fuses or 3 liquid burning flares.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Emergency Equipment

question: Before each trip carrying cargo, what must a truck driver confirm?
choice_a: That the truck is not overloaded and the cargo is balanced and secured
choice_b: That the cargo has a tracking barcode
choice_c: That the cargo is insured
choice_d: That the cargo is refrigerated
explanation: The manual states you must make sure the truck is not overloaded and the cargo is balanced and secured before each trip.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Cargo (Trucks)

question: Spare electrical fuses must be carried as emergency equipment unless the vehicle is:
choice_b: Equipped with dual rear wheels
choice_c: Equipped with circuit breakers
choice_d: A diesel-powered vehicle
explanation: The manual notes spare electrical fuses are required unless the vehicle has circuit breakers.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.3 What to Look For - Emergency Equipment

question: What is the purpose of reviewing the last vehicle inspection report in Step 1?
choice_a: To find the vehicle's purchase price
choice_b: To check the vehicle's odometer reading
choice_c: To verify the driver's license number
choice_d: To confirm the motor carrier repaired or certified as unnecessary any noted defects
explanation: The manual explains the motor carrier must repair items in the report affecting safety and certify repairs were made or unnecessary; you sign only if that certification is in order.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 1

question: Before raising the hood or tilting the cab in Step 2, what should you first check?
choice_a: That the parking brakes are on and/or wheels are chocked
choice_b: That the headlights are on
choice_c: That the engine is running
choice_d: That the parking brake is released
explanation: Step 2 instructs you to check that the parking brakes are on and/or wheels are chocked before raising the hood or tilting the cab.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 2

question: During Step 3, air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within how many minutes?
choice_b: 1 minute
choice_c: 10 minutes
choice_d: 3 minutes
explanation: The manual states air pressure should build from 50 to 90 psi within 3 minutes.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 3

question: The air pressure governor cut-out is usually around what range?
explanation: The manual states you should build air pressure to the governor cut-out, usually around 120-140 psi.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 3

question: If the ABS indicator light stays on after starting the engine, what does this mean?
choice_a: The ABS is not working properly
choice_b: The ABS is functioning perfectly
choice_c: The engine oil is low
choice_d: The parking brake is engaged
explanation: The manual explains the ABS dash light should come on then turn off; if it stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 3

question: For trailers only, what indicates the trailer's ABS is not working properly?
choice_a: A red light on the dashboard flashes
choice_b: The brake pedal vibrates
choice_c: The horn sounds continuously
choice_d: A yellow light on the left rear of the trailer stays on
explanation: The manual states that for trailers, if the yellow light on the left rear of the trailer stays on, the ABS is not working properly.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 3

question: In Step 4, before beginning the walk-around inspection, what should you do?
choice_b: Set the parking brake, turn off the engine, take the key, and turn on low beams and four-way flashers
choice_c: Disconnect the trailer
choice_d: Leave the engine running with all lights off
explanation: Step 4 instructs you to set the parking brake, turn off the engine, take the key, turn on headlights (low beams) and four-way emergency flashers, then get out of the vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 4

question: Which turn signal should be turned on before you begin the walk-around inspection?
choice_b: Both simultaneously
choice_c: The left turn signal
choice_d: Neither
explanation: The manual instructs to turn on the right turn signal and start the walk-around inspection.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 5

question: What should you use to test rust-streaked lug nuts during the walk-around inspection?
choice_b: A tire gauge
choice_c: A flashlight
choice_d: A screwdriver
explanation: The manual instructs to use a wrench to test rust-streaked lug nuts, which indicate looseness.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 5

question: Drivers of trucks and truck tractors transporting cargo must inspect cargo securement within the first how many miles of a trip?
choice_b: 50 miles
choice_c: 250 miles
choice_d: 100 miles
explanation: The manual states drivers must inspect the securement of cargo within the first 50 miles of a trip.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.6 Inspection during a Trip

question: After the initial cargo check, how often must cargo securement be re-inspected?
choice_b: Only at fuel stops
choice_c: Every 500 miles only
choice_d: Every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first
explanation: The manual states re-inspection is required every 150 miles or every three hours, whichever comes first.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.6 Inspection during a Trip

question: In Step 7, how do you test for hydraulic brake leaks?
choice_a: Pump the brake pedal three times, then apply firm pressure and hold for five seconds; the pedal should not move
choice_b: Apply the brake once lightly and release
choice_c: Check only the tire pressure
choice_d: Rev the engine to full throttle while braking
explanation: The manual instructs pumping the brake pedal three times, then applying firm pressure and holding for five seconds; if the pedal moves, there may be a leak.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 7

question: How do you test whether the parking brake holds during Step 7?
choice_a: Slam on the accelerator at full throttle
choice_b: Turn off the engine and coast
choice_c: Gently pull forward against the set parking brake
choice_d: Release all brakes and coast downhill
explanation: The manual instructs to place the vehicle in a low gear and gently pull forward against the parking brake to make sure it holds.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 7

question: At approximately what speed should you test service brake stopping action?
choice_b: About 25 mph
choice_c: About five miles per hour
choice_d: About 55 mph
explanation: The manual instructs to go about five miles per hour and push the brake pedal firmly to test service brake stopping action.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 7

question: What can "pulling" to one side or the other mean when you push the brake pedal?
choice_b: A properly working brake system
choice_c: Brake trouble
choice_d: Good tire pressure
explanation: The manual warns that pulling to one side or the other can mean brake trouble.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.1.5 Seven-step Inspection Method, Step 7

question: How should you keep from rolling back when starting with a manual transmission?
choice_b: Partly engage the clutch before releasing the brake, or use the parking brake/trailer hand valve as needed
choice_c: Fully release the clutch immediately
choice_d: Accelerate hard immediately with the clutch out
explanation: The manual advises partly engaging the clutch before releasing the brake, and using the parking brake or a trailer hand valve to prevent rolling back.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: Why should you speed up smoothly and gradually?
choice_a: It is required by law with no safety purpose
choice_b: It prevents the radio from picking up static
choice_c: Rough acceleration can cause mechanical damage and, when pulling a trailer, can damage the coupling
choice_d: It only affects fuel economy
explanation: The manual states rough acceleration can cause mechanical damage and, when pulling a trailer, can damage the coupling.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: When traction is poor, such as in rain or snow, what should you do if the drive wheels begin to spin?
choice_b: Take your foot off the accelerator
choice_c: Shift to a higher gear immediately
choice_d: Press the accelerator harder
explanation: The manual instructs that if the drive wheels begin to spin, take your foot off the accelerator.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.1 Accelerating

question: How should you hold the steering wheel?
choice_b: With both hands at the very bottom of the wheel
choice_c: With your palm resting on top only
choice_d: Firmly with both hands on opposite sides of the wheel
explanation: The manual instructs holding the steering wheel firmly with both hands on opposite sides so it doesn't pull away from your hands if you hit a curb or pothole.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.2 Steering

question: When stopping, how should you push the brake pedal?
choice_a: Down gradually, controlling pressure for a smooth, safe stop
choice_b: As hard as possible every time
choice_c: With short rapid taps only
choice_d: Using only the parking brake
explanation: The manual instructs pushing the brake pedal down gradually and controlling pressure so the vehicle comes to a smooth, safe stop.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.3 Stopping

question: Why is backing always dangerous?
choice_a: Because it wears out the tires faster
choice_b: Because it is illegal in most states
choice_c: Because it uses significantly more fuel
choice_d: Because you cannot see everything behind your vehicle
explanation: The manual states backing is always dangerous because you cannot see everything behind your vehicle.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: When you must back, which direction should you back and turn toward whenever possible?
choice_b: The passenger's side
choice_c: The driver's side
choice_d: It does not matter which side
explanation: The manual advises backing and turning toward the driver's side whenever possible.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Why is backing toward the driver's side preferred over the right side?
choice_b: It is required by federal law in all states
choice_c: You can watch the rear of your vehicle by looking out the side window
choice_d: It reduces fuel consumption
explanation: The manual explains that backing toward the driver's side lets you watch the rear of your vehicle by looking out the side window, since backing toward the right is very dangerous.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Before backing, what should you do to check your path?
choice_a: Get out and walk around the vehicle to check clearance to the sides and overhead
choice_b: Rely solely on a backup camera
choice_c: Only glance quickly in the mirror
choice_d: Ask a passenger to guess the clearance
explanation: The manual advises getting out and walking around the vehicle to check clearance to the sides and overhead in and near the path the vehicle will take.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: When using a helper while backing, what should be agreed upon beforehand?
choice_b: A set of hand signals, including a signal for "stop"
choice_c: Nothing; helpers should improvise as needed
choice_d: The route for the entire remaining trip
explanation: The manual instructs working out a set of hand signals that both driver and helper understand, and agreeing on a signal for "stop."
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: How fast should you back your vehicle?
choice_b: As slowly as possible, using the lowest reverse gear
choice_c: As fast as safely possible to minimize exposure
choice_d: At highway speed
explanation: The manual instructs backing as slowly as possible and using the lowest reverse gear so you can correct steering errors or stop quickly.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.2.4 Backing Safely

question: Most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require what technique to change gears?
choice_b: Single clutching
choice_c: No clutching at all
choice_d: Clutch braking only
explanation: The manual states most heavy vehicles with unsynchronized manual transmissions require double clutching to change gears.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: If a vehicle has a synchronized manual transmission, is double clutching required?
choice_b: No, it is not required
choice_c: Yes, it is always required
choice_d: Only when downshifting
explanation: The manual states that if equipped with a synchronized manual transmission, double clutching is not required.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: What are the two ways of knowing when to shift up?
choice_a: Using the fuel gauge and oil pressure gauge
choice_b: Using engine speed (rpm) via the tachometer, or using road speed (mph) via the speedometer
choice_c: Using the horn and headlights
choice_d: Using the clock and the odometer
explanation: The manual describes using engine speed (rpm) and using road speed (mph) as the two ways of knowing when to shift up.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: What is "progressive shifting" as described for some newer vehicles?
choice_b: Fully automatic shifting with no driver input
choice_c: Shifting only every other gear
choice_d: The rpm at which you shift becomes higher as you move up in the gears
explanation: The manual explains that with progressive shifting, the rpm at which you shift becomes higher as you move up in the gears.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions

question: Why should you downshift before starting down a hill?
choice_a: So you can control speed without using the brakes hard, preventing brake overheating
choice_b: It is required at every hill regardless of grade
choice_c: To make the ride smoother for passengers
choice_d: To conserve fuel only
explanation: The manual explains you should slow down and shift down before a hill to a speed you can control without using the brakes hard, otherwise brakes can overheat and lose braking power.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions - Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

question: Why should you downshift to the right gear before entering a curve?
choice_a: It lets you use some power through the curve for stability and speed up as soon as you're out of it
choice_b: It prevents the horn from working
choice_c: It has no real safety benefit
choice_d: It only helps with fuel economy
explanation: The manual explains downshifting before a curve lets you use some power through the curve to help the vehicle be more stable and allows you to speed up as soon as you're out of the curve.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.1 Manual Transmissions - Basic Procedures for Shifting Down

question: What typically controls multi-speed rear axles and auxiliary transmissions?
choice_a: A selector knob or switch on the gearshift lever of the main transmission
choice_b: The cruise control stalk
choice_c: The parking brake lever
choice_d: A foot pedal only
explanation: The manual states these are usually controlled by a selector knob or switch on the gearshift lever of the main transmission.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.2 Multi-speed Rear Axles and Auxiliary Transmissions

question: In an automatic transmission, what does selecting a low range going down a grade do?
choice_b: Increases fuel consumption with no other effect
choice_c: Locks the vehicle in park
choice_d: Prevents the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear, providing greater engine braking
explanation: The manual explains lower ranges prevent the transmission from shifting up beyond the selected gear, giving greater engine braking on grades.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.3 Automatic Transmissions

question: How many basic types of retarders does the manual describe?
choice_b: Four (exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric)
choice_c: One
choice_d: Two
explanation: The manual states there are four basic types of retarders: exhaust, engine, hydraulic, and electric.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.4 Retarders

question: When should you turn a retarder off?
choice_a: Whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered
choice_b: Only when going uphill
choice_c: Retarders should never be turned off
choice_d: Only in hot weather
explanation: The manual warns to turn the retarder off whenever the road is wet, icy, or snow covered, because poor traction may cause the drive wheels to skid.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.3.4 Retarders

question: How far ahead should most good drivers look?
choice_b: 30 to 45 seconds
choice_c: At least 12 to 15 seconds
choice_d: 2 to 3 seconds
explanation: The manual states most good drivers look at least 12 to 15 seconds ahead.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead

question: At highway speeds, looking 12-15 seconds ahead covers about what distance?
choice_b: About one block
choice_c: About a quarter of a mile
choice_d: About 50 feet
explanation: The manual states at highway speeds, 12-15 seconds ahead is about a quarter of a mile.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead

question: At lower speeds, looking 12-15 seconds ahead covers about what distance?
choice_b: About one block
choice_c: About a quarter mile
choice_d: About 10 miles
explanation: The manual states at lower speeds, 12-15 seconds ahead is about one block.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.1 Seeing Ahead

question: When should mirror adjustment be checked, and under what condition can it only be checked accurately?
choice_a: Prior to the start of any trip, and only accurately when the trailer(s) are straight
choice_b: Only when changing drivers mid-route
choice_c: Only once a year, regardless of trailer position
choice_d: Only after a crash
explanation: The manual states mirror adjustment should be checked prior to the start of any trip and can only be checked accurately when the trailer(s) are straight.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: What should each mirror be adjusted to show?
choice_a: Only the ground directly behind the vehicle
choice_b: Only the sky
choice_c: Nothing but the oncoming traffic lane
choice_d: Some part of the vehicle, to give a reference point for judging other images
explanation: The manual advises adjusting mirrors to show some part of the vehicle, giving a reference point for judging the position of other images.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: Besides traffic, what else can you use your mirrors to check?
choice_a: Your tires (to spot a tire fire) and open cargo such as loose straps or a flapping tarp
choice_b: The engine oil level
choice_c: The transmission fluid level
choice_d: The battery charge indicator
explanation: The manual states you can use mirrors to keep an eye on your tires to spot a tire fire, and to check open cargo for loose straps, ropes, chains, or a flapping/ballooning tarp.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear

question: According to the manual, at how many points during a lane change should you check your mirrors?
choice_a: Only after completing the lane change
choice_b: Mirrors are not needed during lane changes
choice_c: Only once, before starting
choice_d: Before signaling, after signaling, right after starting the change, and after completing it
explanation: The manual lists checking mirrors before changing lanes, after signaling, right after starting the change, and after completing the lane change.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear - Special Situations

question: What is true of convex ("fisheye," "bug-eye") mirrors?
choice_a: They are illegal on commercial vehicles
choice_b: They make objects appear closer than they really are
choice_c: They show a narrower area than flat mirrors
choice_d: They show a wider area, but objects appear smaller and farther away than they really are
explanation: The manual explains convex mirrors show a wider area but everything appears smaller and farther away than it really is.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.4.2 Seeing to the Sides and Rear - How to Use Mirrors

question: What are the three good rules for using turn signals?
choice_a: Signal loudly, signal briefly, and signal randomly
choice_b: Only signal for left turns
choice_c: Signal early, signal continuously, and cancel your signal
choice_d: Signal only at night
explanation: The manual gives three rules for turn signals: signal early, signal continuously, and cancel your signal.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions - Turns

question: How can you warn drivers behind you that you're slowing down?
choice_b: Turning off all your lights
choice_c: Speeding up briefly
choice_d: A few light taps on the brake pedal to flash the brake lights
explanation: The manual advises a few light taps on the brake pedal, enough to flash the brake lights, to warn following drivers.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions - Slowing Down

question: When should you use four-way emergency flashers, according to the communicating section?
choice_a: When driving very slowly or when stopped
choice_b: During a normal, routine lane change
choice_c: At every intersection
choice_d: While accelerating onto a highway
explanation: The manual states to use four-way emergency flashers for times when driving very slowly or stopped.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.5.1 Signal Your Intentions - Slowing Down

question: Why shouldn't you try to direct traffic, such as signaling another driver that it's safe to pass?
choice_a: It saves the other driver time with no risk
choice_b: It's encouraged as a professional courtesy

question: Why must you check that defrosters and heaters work before winter driving?
choice_a: They have no real safety relevance

question: Why is having enough tire tread especially important in winter conditions?

choice_b: Drive tires must provide traction through wet pavement and snow, and steering tires must have traction to steer
choice_c: It only matters for fuel efficiency
choice_d: It is only a cosmetic consideration
explanation: The manual explains drive tires must provide traction to push the rig over wet pavement and through snow, and steering tires must have traction to steer, making tread especially important in winter.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.13.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: Why should you learn how to put on tire chains before you actually need them?
choice_a: Chains may only be installed by a certified mechanic
choice_b: Chains are never actually needed on commercial vehicles
choice_c: So you're prepared and know how, rather than learning under pressure in snow and ice
choice_d: It's only a minor suggestion with no real benefit
explanation: The manual advises learning how to put chains on before you need to do it in snow and ice.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.13.1 Vehicle Checks - Tire Chains

question: When starting to drive on slippery roads, what should you do?

question: What indicates that ice may have formed on the road ahead?

source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.13.2 Driving - Check for Ice

question: On slippery surfaces, why should you avoid using the engine brake or speed retarder?
choice_a: They have no effect on skidding

choice_c: They wear out faster in cold weather
choice_d: They consume more fuel in winter
explanation: The manual warns not to use the engine brake or speed retarder on slippery surfaces because they can cause the driving wheels to skid.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.13.2 Driving - Adjust Turning and Braking to Conditions

question: On slippery roads, how should you adjust your following distance and lane position?
choice_a: Keep a longer following distance and don't drive alongside other vehicles
choice_b: Drive alongside others for safety in numbers

choice_d: Following distance does not need to change

question: What problems can wet brakes cause?

question: When crossing deep standing water, what should you do with your brakes?
choice_a: Avoid touching the brakes at all while crossing
choice_b: Fully release the parking brake while crossing
choice_c: Slam on the brakes to test them before crossing
choice_d: Gently apply the brakes to keep mud, silt, sand, and water from getting into them

source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.13.2 Driving - Wet Brakes

question: After crossing deep water, what should you do to dry out your brakes?
choice_b: Apply maximum brake pressure while accelerating hard
choice_c: Maintain light pressure on the brakes for a short distance to heat and dry them
choice_d: Turn off the engine and wait several minutes
explanation: The manual instructs maintaining light pressure on the brakes for a short distance after crossing water to heat them up and dry them out.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.13.2 Driving - Wet Brakes

question: In very hot weather, how often should you inspect your tires?
choice_b: Every two hours or every 100 miles
choice_c: Only at the start of the trip
choice_d: Once per day only
explanation: The manual advises inspecting tires every two hours or every 100 miles when driving in very hot weather.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: If a tire is too hot to touch, what should you do?
choice_a: Add more air to the tire immediately
choice_b: Remain stopped until the tire cools off
choice_c: Let air out to cool it faster
choice_d: Continue driving at a reduced speed
explanation: The manual instructs remaining stopped until a too-hot-to-touch tire cools off, otherwise it may blow out or catch fire.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: Why shouldn't you let air out of a hot tire to lower its pressure?
choice_a: It has no effect on the tire either way
choice_b: It will make the tire cooler immediately
choice_c: The pressure will be too low once the tire cools off
choice_d: It is required by federal regulation
explanation: The manual warns not to let air out because air pressure increases with temperature, and letting air out will leave the pressure too low once the tire cools off.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Tires

question: Before removing a radiator cap from a pressurized cooling system, what must you do?
choice_a: Remove it while the engine is still running

choice_d: Wait until the system has cooled, since steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns
explanation: The manual warns never to remove the radiator cap until the system has cooled, because steam and boiling water can spray under pressure and cause severe burns.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Engine Coolant

question: When adding coolant to a system without a recovery or overflow tank, what is one of the first steps?
choice_a: Keep the engine running at high rpm
choice_b: Shut the engine off and wait until it has cooled
choice_c: Add coolant while continuing to drive
choice_d: Disconnect the vehicle's battery first
explanation: The manual's steps for adding coolant to a system without a recovery tank begin with shutting the engine off and waiting until it has cooled.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.14.1 Vehicle Checks - Engine Coolant

question: What can cause an engine to overheat, according to the section on engine belts?

question: What is "bleeding tar," and why is it a hazard in hot weather?

question: Why should you avoid high speeds in hot or desert conditions?

choice_c: There is no added risk from speed in hot weather
choice_d: High speeds keep the engine running cooler
explanation: The manual warns high speeds create more heat for tires and the engine, and in desert conditions this heat increases chances of tire failure, fire, or engine failure.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.14.2 Driving - Go Slowly Enough to Prevent Overheating

question: What is a "passive" railroad crossing?

choice_b: A crossing that is permanently closed to traffic

choice_d: A crossing without any traffic control device, where the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely with the driver
explanation: The manual defines a passive crossing as one without any traffic control device, where the decision to stop or proceed rests entirely in the driver's hands.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.15.1 Types of Crossings

question: What is an "active" railroad crossing?
choice_a: A crossing with a traffic control device such as flashing lights, bells, or gates
choice_b: A crossing used only by freight trains
choice_c: A crossing with no signage of any kind
choice_d: A crossing with a stop sign but no other devices
explanation: The manual defines an active crossing as one with a traffic control device installed to regulate traffic, including flashing red lights with or without bells and gates.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.15.1 Types of Crossings

question: What does the round, black-on-yellow advance warning sign tell you to do?

question: Which vehicles are required to stop at every public railroad crossing, per the manual?

choice_c: Only vehicles longer than 40 feet
choice_d: Only empty trucks

source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.15.2 Warning Signs and Devices - Advance Warning Signs

question: If there is no white stop line at a cross-buck crossing, how close may a vehicle required to stop be positioned relative to the nearest rail?

question: What does a sign posted below a cross-buck indicate?

question: When flashing red lights begin at a railroad crossing, what should you do?
choice_a: Speed up to cross before the train arrives

source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.15.2 Warning Signs and Devices - Flashing Red Light Signals

question: At a crossing with gates, when should you stop and how long should you remain stopped?
choice_a: Only stop if a train is visibly approaching

explanation: The manual instructs stopping when lights begin to flash and before the gate lowers, remaining stopped until the gates go up and lights stop flashing.
source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.15.2 Warning Signs and Devices - Gates

question: Why is it dangerous to assume you're clear after checking only one track on a double-track crossing?
choice_a: Trains cannot travel on both tracks simultaneously

source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.15.3 Driving Procedures - Double Tracks Require a Double Check

question: Should you rely solely on warning signals, gates, or flagmen at a railroad crossing?

choice_b: Only gates need to be trusted
choice_c: Only flashing lights need to be trusted

question: What is your most important consideration when selecting a safe speed for a downgrade?
choice_a: A speed that is not too fast for the vehicle's weight, the grade's length/steepness, road conditions, and weather
choice_b: Using only the parking brake regardless of speed

question: What should be the principal way of controlling your speed on a mountain downgrade?

source_note: Nebraska Commercial Driver's License Manual, Section 2 - Driving Safely, 2.16.1 Select a "Safe" Speed

question: Why must you shift to a low gear before starting down a grade, rather than after speed has built up?

choice_b: It's only a minor suggestion with no real risk
choice_c: It saves fuel with no safety implication

question: What happens to brakes on a long, steep downgrade if they are overused and become too hot?

question: Why must brake adjustment be checked frequently, especially on vehicles used a lot?

choice_b: Only new brakes need adjustment checks

choice_d: Adjustment has no real effect on brake performance

question: Why should you know the locations of escape ramps on your route in advance?
choice_a: They are reserved only for use by emergency vehicles
choice_b: So you can use them if your brakes fail on a downgrade, since they save lives, equipment, and cargo
